item.title: People Who Write Interestingly
item.description:
I want to share a collection of people on the internet who write interesting content on product-adjacent topics and are worth reading. I often find myself returning to articles by these authors — especially during moments when I’m looking for creative inspiration.

  • Marty Cagan — an iconic figure in the product world and author of a series of widely read books: Inspired, Empowered, and Transformed. Founder of SVPG and a prolific blogger on product management. His ideas about product discovery and empowered teams have become industry standards.
  • Paul Graham — co-founder of Y Combinator and author of remarkable essays that remain relevant across time. He writes about startups, thinking, and decision-making — concisely, precisely, and without filler.
  • Andrew Chen — partner at Andreessen Horowitz and author of a popular blog on growth marketing.
  • Vitalik Buterin — founder of Ethereum and an active blogger. He writes deep technical and philosophical essays on decentralization and the future of technology.
  • Grigory Bakunov — founder of radio-t, former Director of Technology Outreach at Yandex. Writes about technology, management, and life in tech — sharply and without corporate-speak.
  • Oleg Yakubenkov — founder of GoPractice and author of the most popular blog on product analytics in the Russian-speaking world. His simulators and articles are must-reads for anyone who wants to get serious about metrics and unit economics.
  • Artem Gorbunov & Co. — a collection of useful advice on product topics from renowned specialists. Short and to the point — covering writing, interfaces, negotiation, and management.
  • Melissa Perri — author of Escaping the Build Trap. Writes about product as a value system, product culture, and why companies get stuck in feature factory mode.
  • Teresa Torres — author of Continuous Discovery Habits. Her blog covers discovery practices: opportunity solution trees, customer interviews, and the habits of strong product teams.
  • Wes Kao — runs an excellent, practical blog on management, product thinking, and career development. Publishes regularly.
  • Ben Thompson — technology analyst and author of the Stratechery blog. Digs deep into the business strategies of tech companies, platform models, and competitive market dynamics.
  • Valeria Rozova — product leader and curator of an article library on product topics, written by graduates of her courses. The articles are highly practical and detailed — a great resource for developing specific product skills.

item.title: Books and Resources for Product Managers
item.description:
There’s no shortage of materials online for developing product skills and broadening your horizons. But I want to bring together the most useful, practical, and valuable ones. This list is continuously improving — new materials get added, outdated ones removed. I hope you find something worth your time.

Introduction to Product Culture and the Profession

  • Essay «How to Do Great Work,» Paul Graham. An essay by the iconic Paul Graham on how to do your work well — full of advice and reflection. Recommended reading for anyone starting out in their career, not just product managers.
  • Article «Good Product Manager / Bad Product Manager,» Ben Horowitz. A short piece written in 2012 that remains just as relevant today. It gives a solid general picture of what qualities a good product manager should have.
  • Article «Amazon Leadership Principles,» Amazon. Amazon’s 14 leadership principles — the standard expected of managers at the company and a mandatory part of their interview process. If they don’t resonate with you on the first read, it’s worth coming back to them later.

Managing Yourself and Your Teams

  • «Getting Things Done,» David Allen
  • «Jedi Techniques,» Maxim Dorofeev
  • «Herding Cats: A Primer for Programmers Who Lead Programmers,» J. Hank Rainwater
  • «Managing Humans: Biting and Humorous Tales of a Software Engineering Manager,» Michael Lopp

Research

  • «The Mom Test,» Rob Fitzpatrick. Essential reading on customer discovery interviews. People have strong opinions about the approach in this book — some love it, some push back — but everyone’s read it and no one was left indifferent.
  • «Running Lean: Iterate from Plan A to a Plan That Works,» Ash Maurya
  • Video «How to Talk to Users,» Eric Migicovsky (Y Combinator)
  • Video «ABCDX Segmentation,» Artem Azevich (IIDF Accelerator)
  • Video «Market Sizing,» Alexander Skurikhin (IIDF Accelerator, Yandex)
  • producthunt.com

Analytics

  • «Playing the Numbers: How Analytics Helps Video Games Thrive,» Vasily Sabirov. Probably the only book on product analytics written by a Russian author. It reads less like a textbook and more like a conversation with a product analyst.
  • «Say It with Charts: The Executive’s Guide to Visual Communication,» Gene Zelazny
  • GoPractice Blog. Simply an encyclopedia of product analytics and product management knowledge. Exceptionally well-written articles. Best enjoyed slowly, in the evening, over a cup of tea.
  • Free course «Fundamentals of Statistics and A/B Testing» by Yandex Practicum. An excellent introduction to statistics and A/B testing, put together by Practicum’s team of mathematicians.
  • Free course «Fundamentals of Statistics» by Anatoly Karpov. The most popular statistics course in the Russian-speaking internet, where Anatoly walks through both descriptive and inferential statistics in a clear, structured way. It has become a classic in the Russian-language learning community.

Strategy

  • «Good Strategy Bad Strategy,» Richard Rumelt. A foundational book on strategy that explains what good strategy looks like — and what the many bad versions look like. There’s a short summary on my blog.
  • «The Goal: A Process of Ongoing Improvement,» Eliyahu Goldratt

Delivery Management / Backlog Management

  • «Getting Real: The Smarter, Faster, Easier Way to Build a Successful Web Application,» Jason Fried + David Heinemeier Hansson + Matthew Linderman
  • Article «20 Product Prioritization Techniques: A Map and Guided Tour». A detailed overview of 20 techniques for prioritizing your backlog or hypotheses.
  • Article «RICE: Simple prioritization for product managers,» Intercom. The original article from Intercom, where this prioritization method was born. It also includes an Excel template you can put to use right away.

Interviews and Hiring

  • «The Art of Recruitment: How to Evaluate a Person in an Hour,» Svetlana Ivanova
  • «Who: The A Method for Hiring,» Geoff Smart and Randy Street
  • «Cracking the PM Interview: How to Land a Product Manager Job in Technology,» Gayle Laakmann McDowell
  • «Decode and Conquer,» Lewis C. Lin. One of Lewis Lin’s books — read the others too if you can.
  • Podcast «Sobes» (Interview)
  • Podcast «Dva Stula» (Two Chairs)

Computer Science Basics

  • Free Python courses «Generation Python». A series of free Python courses from scratch by professional developer and instructor Timur Guev. Timur comes from a generation of mathematicians who scored perfect marks on Russia’s national university entrance exams and a generation of developers who went on to work at FAANG companies. You won’t find better beginner courses than this series.
  • Free SQL trainer at sql-ex.ru. One of the best — if not the best — SQL practice platforms, and it’s free. It has an enormous number of exercises; I recommend working through them to build solid SQL query skills. Don’t let the dated interface put you off.
  • «System Design Interview,» Alex Xu

Data Science Basics

  • Article «Machine Learning for People,» vas3k. A thorough introduction for anyone who wants to finally make sense of machine learning — written in plain language, without formulas or theorems, with real-world examples and solutions.
  • «Machine Learning for Humans,» Vishal Maini, Samir Sabri

Inspiring Stories

  • «Elon Musk: Tesla, SpaceX, and the Quest for a Fantastic Future,» Ashlee Vance. The story of Musk’s rise as an entrepreneur — the obstacles he overcame, the risks he took. Including his trip to Russia in 2001 and his attempt to buy an intercontinental ballistic missile.
  • «Pour Your Heart Into It: How Starbucks Built a Company One Cup at a Time,» Dori Jones Yang, Howard Schultz
  • «The Yandex Book,» Dmitry Sokolov-Mitrich. The story of Yandex’s rise from its origins to its IPO. About the personalities of its founders. About how Sergey Brin and Larry Page came to Moscow in 2003 to acquire the company, but Arkady Volozh and Ilya Segalovich refused to sell — and went on to build the most technologically advanced IT company in Russia.
